P.B.S. Pinchback. Pinckney Benton Stewart Pinchback was Louisiana's most prominent Black Reconstruction politician, serving as acting governor in 1872 and as a United States senator and congressman. A riverboat captain and political organizer of extraordinary ambition, he navigated the treacherous rapids of Reconstruction politics with agility and resolve.

Pinchback served as acting governor of Louisiana from 1872 to 1873, the only Black governor of the Reconstruction era, though his legitimacy was contested and his tenure cut short. In 1873, he was elected to the U.S. Senate, though his seat was challenged and never formally confirmed due to Democratic obstruction and recounts. He later served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1875 to 1876, representing a Louisiana district under Republican Reconstruction until Democratic Redemption ended his seat.

Before the war, Pinchback was a riverboat captain who accumulated wealth and political networks rapidly during Reconstruction, becoming Louisiana's Republican Party boss. He was known for pragmatic deal-making and coalition-building across racial lines, though he remained unyielding on Black suffrage and civil rights. Though his tenure in high office was brief, he remained politically active after Reconstruction and served as U.S. Marshal for the Eastern District of Louisiana, extending his influence beyond the Reconstruction era.
